era_visual_canon.clothing: Mining-era workforce (1937-1966): miners and mill hands in sweat-stained cotton work shirts or sleeveless singlets, khaki or drill work trousers and shorts, heavy leather work boots and wide-brimmed felt or cloth hats, at most a simple cloth dust mask, with clothing and skin coated in fine fibrous dust. Company managers, mines inspectors and public health doctors wear lightweight suits or shirtsleeves with ties, trousers and leather shoes. Migrant wives wear modest knee-length cotton dresses and cardigans, and children wear shorts, simple frocks and sandals or go barefoot. Later decades: 1970s-1990s casual Australian rural clothing and plain business suits for officials, lawyers and politicians. From 2008, environmental officers wear modern protective gear behind barricades, and Banjima traditional owners and advocates wear contemporary casual or formal clothing at hearings and press events.
era_visual_canon.technology: 1937-1966: crushers, ore mills, belt conveyors and bagging plants with rudimentary dust-extraction equipment added late; manual typewriters, carbon-copy paper reports and handwritten letters; wall-mounted crank or rotary telephones; valve radios; film cameras and black-and-white or sepia prints; hospital forceps and basic mid-century medical instruments. NO plastic-cased electronics, NO digital displays, NO powered respirators, NO air-monitoring electronics. 1980s-1990s: fax machines, early desktop computers, CRT televisions. From 2008: digital mapping, laptops and modern sampling gear in remediation contexts only.
era_visual_canon.vehicles_machinery: 1937-1966: dusty flatbed and tipper trucks hauling tailings, early utility vehicles and four-wheel-drive field vehicles on unsealed red-earth tracks, ore-processing mill plant beside the gorge, and small propeller-driven passenger aircraft on a bare tailings-surfaced airstrip. Migrant arrival by ocean passenger liner from Málaga through the Suez Canal. Later decades: 1970s-1990s sedans and 4WDs, and demolition excavators of 1986-1992. From 2008: modern 4WD government vehicles stopped at permanent barricades.
era_visual_canon.interiors: 1937-1966: sparse company houses of corrugated iron, timber and fibro-cement sheeting with simple furniture, louvred windows, ceiling fans and dust on every surface; a basic single-room-style school; a small town hospital with iron beds and white-enamel fittings; a noisy mill interior thick with suspended fibre dust; plain government offices with filing cabinets and typewriters. Later: courtrooms and parliamentary hearing rooms in timber panelling (1988-1994); family living rooms in Madrid with sepia family photographs on display (interview setting).
era_visual_canon.forbidden_anachronisms: In 1937-1966 scenes: no hi-vis vests, no hard hats with modern logos, no modern P2/P3 respirators or hazmat suits, no sealed asphalt with painted road lines, no plastic water bottles, no smartphones or digital screens, no modern 4WD SUVs, no jet aircraft at the airstrip, no warning signs or barricades (these belong only to the post-2006 forbidden zone). In demolished-era scenes, do not show the town as intact or populated.
era_visual_canon.materials_textures: Company dwellings of corrugated iron, timber and fibro-cement (asbestos-cement) sheeting; loose, crumbly, fibrous crocidolite mine tailings spread and compacted as the surface of roads, the airstrip, house yards, the school playground and public spaces; raw fibrous asbestos that frays into threads and sheds a fine powder when handled; a fine fibrous dust coating people, buildings and machinery; tailings dumps in rocky gorge walls; asbestos deposits settled in creek beds, pools and alluvial floodplains.
era_visual_canon.color_palette: Exterior: intense red-ochre earth and red dust everywhere, blue-grey crocidolite tailings on roads, yards and dumps (INFERENCE from 'blue asbestos'), dull grey corrugated iron and pale grey fibro walls under a harsh bright desert sky; interior colours not documented.
era_visual_canon.scale_dimensions: The official Wittenoom Asbestos Management Area covers 46,840 hectares. More than three million tonnes of tailings were left behind after three mines produced about 150,000 tonnes of commercial asbestos (1937-1966). Contamination extends downstream through creeks, pools and floodplains toward the Fortescue River catchment. The town is small and isolated, with a small-aircraft airstrip; building heights and footprints are not documented (INFERENCE: low single-storey structures).
era_visual_canon.distinctive_features: An isolated red-earth Pilbara mining town whose roads, yards, school playground and airstrip were literally paved with crumbling blue crocidolite tailings, set beside gorges choked with tailings dumps. Today it is emptied, demolished and sealed off by permanent barricades as a 46,840-hectare forbidden contamination zone.
era_visual_canon.demographics: Mining-era population (1937-1966): a predominantly male, high-turnover workforce of miners, mill hands and fitters, with 59% leaving within six months. It combined Australian workers, post-war European displaced persons assigned 1948-1951, CSR-recruited Europeans from 1950, and Spanish migrants arriving under the 1958 Spain-Australia agreement, accompanied by wives and young children; workers appear in dust-coated work clothes. Australian company managers, government mines and health officials and union representatives appear as visitors and authorities. Banjima Aboriginal traditional owners hold the land, documented as claimants and activists in 2023-2026. Composition comes from written and oral records, not photographs.
era_visual_canon.visual_reference_availability: No [VISUAL] source block was supplied; every place detail is TEXT-sourced. Oral testimony: a former child resident's memories supply the small propeller plane, red earth, dust everywhere, tin/timber/fibro-cement houses and children fraying asbestos. A former worker's testimony supplies the tailings spread on yards, accesses, schools, kindergarten and churches. Official written records supply the 1957 Board of Reference dust cloud at the mill and the 1965 playground tailings reprimand. Technical and environmental reports supply the tailings tonnage, 46,840 ha area, and deposits in creeks, pools and floodplains. An official government notice supplies the permanent barricades. The only photographic sources mentioned are private family albums: a portrait showing a bandaged foot, a photo dated 1963-07-07 linked to a baptism, and sepia family photographs seen in an interview. None are reproduced in the pool. Tailings colour is inferred from 'blue asbestos'; interior colours and building dimensions are undocumented.

condition_evolution.at_event: During the mining era (1937-1966) the town is inhabited and operating. The mill stands under a thick suspended dust cloud with dust-covered workers, trucks dump fresh tailings onto yards and roads, children play on tailings-surfaced ground, and houses of tin, timber and fibro-cement sit on red earth with fine dust coating everything.
condition_evolution.later: From 1978 the town is deliberately run down. Buildings are demolished and the school, nursing post and police station close (1986-1992); the airport closes (1993); power is cut (2006); the town is abolished and erased from maps and signs (2007, some sources 2006); the last residents leave and final structures are demolished (2022-2023). Wind and water erode the tailings into creeks and floodplains, and permanent barricades block the town and gorge entrances.

periods.clothing: Prospectors and early miners in rough cotton shirts, singlets, khaki trousers, felt slouch hats and leather boots; inspectors and managers in suits or shirtsleeves with ties; wartime and post-war austerity civilian dress.
periods.technology: Hand tools, early crushing and milling plant, manual typewriters, handwritten and typed reports, wall telephones, valve radios. No dust-control equipment of any effective kind.
periods.vehicles_machinery: Early motor trucks and utility vehicles on unsealed tracks; small mine workings in the Yampire and Wittenoom gorges; a basic early ore mill.
periods.interiors: Rough camp huts and early corrugated-iron dwellings; spartan government and company offices with paper files.

periods.clothing: Multinational workforce in singlets, work shirts, shorts or drill trousers, wide-brim hats and work boots, all coated in dust; Spanish and other European migrant wives in modest cotton dresses; children in shorts and simple frocks; officials in lightweight suits.
periods.technology: Expanded mill plant with conveyors and bagging, dust-reducing equipment installed after 1957, typewriters, rotary telephones, film cameras, mid-century hospital equipment including forceps.
periods.vehicles_machinery: Tipper trucks spreading tailings on roads and yards, utility vehicles, small propeller passenger aircraft on the tailings-surfaced airstrip, ocean liners for migrant arrival.
periods.interiors: Inhabited company houses of tin, timber and fibro-cement; town school, small hospital, churches and a dust-choked mill interior.

periods.clothing: 1970s-1990s casual Australian clothing for remaining residents; business suits for lawyers, judges' robes in court, suits for parliamentarians; ageing former workers in plain civilian clothes.
periods.technology: 1970s-1990s office technology: typewriters, then fax machines and early computers; CRT televisions; film photography.
periods.vehicles_machinery: 1970s-1990s sedans and 4WDs, demolition machinery during 1986-1992, a closed airstrip after 1993.
periods.interiors: Emptying houses with dated furnishings, courtrooms, parliamentary committee rooms, and hospitals where former residents are treated for asbestos disease.

periods.clothing: Contemporary casual and formal clothing for Banjima traditional owners, advocates and lawyers; modern protective suits and respirators only for officials inside the contaminated zone.
periods.technology: Laptops, digital mapping, environmental sampling equipment, modern media cameras at press events.
periods.vehicles_machinery: Modern 4WD vehicles halted at permanent barricades; no operating mine machinery.
periods.interiors: Modern legal offices, Federal Court settings and community meeting rooms.

people_groups.who: Miners, mill hands, fitters and labourers of the Wittenoom crocidolite operations: Australian workers, post-war European displaced persons, CSR-recruited Europeans and Spanish migrants.
people_groups.where_when: Wittenoom mines, gorge and mill from 1937 to 1966, with surviving former workers appearing as ageing disease sufferers and claimants into the 1980s-1990s.
people_groups.appearance: Adult men of European origin (Anglo-Australian, Central and Eastern European, Southern European including Spanish), with fair to olive skin, dark to light hair and lean working builds.

condition_by_period.condition: Covered head to toe in fine fibrous asbestos dust, sunburnt and exhausted from long shifts of up to 16 hours, with occasional untreated injuries such as a bandaged foot wound.
Ageing former workers visibly ill with asbestosis, lung cancer and mesothelioma: breathless, gaunt and frail.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Sweat-stained cotton work shirts or singlets, khaki trousers, leather work boots and felt slouch hats, with no respiratory protection beyond an occasional cloth over the mouth.
Singlets or short-sleeved work shirts, drill shorts or trousers, heavy boots and wide-brimmed cloth hats, short mid-century haircuts, all dust-coated.
Plain civilian shirts, trousers and cardigans of retired working-class men, sometimes in hospital gowns.

people_groups.who: Spanish migrant miners, their wives and children who came to Wittenoom under the 1958 Spain-Australia migration agreement, including children born in the town who later worked in television and film.
people_groups.where_when: On the ship from Málaga via Suez and at the Wittenoom airstrip, houses and hospital in 1962-1964; back in Madrid from 1966 and 1971; at an Australian airport checkpoint in 1985; and as elderly interviewees and adult children in the 2020s.
people_groups.appearance: Spanish people of Mediterranean European origin with olive to light skin, dark brown to black hair and dark eyes.

condition_by_period.condition: Seasick and drained by intense heat during the long sea voyage.
Coated in red earth and fine asbestos dust; children's hands and mouths dusty from fraying raw asbestos; a mother weakened after a kidney infection and a complicated forceps birth.
A former miner rapidly declining with mesothelioma in the months after diagnosis.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Men in work shirts and trousers or dust-covered mine clothing; women in modest knee-length cotton dresses with neatly set early-1960s hair; children in shorts, simple frocks and sandals or barefoot; infants in white baptismal gowns.
Modest late-1960s urban Madrid clothing: men in jackets and trousers, women in skirts and blouses.
A young man in mid-1980s casual travel clothes carrying a passport.
Elderly woman in neat home clothing surrounded by sepia family photographs; adult children in contemporary casual or professional attire.

people_groups.who: General residents of the company town, including families, schoolchildren, the school principal, members of the town steering committee and the last holdouts.
people_groups.where_when: Houses, playground, school, kindergarten and churches of Wittenoom from the 1940s to 1966, then a shrinking remnant population from 1978 until the last residents left in 2022-2023.

condition_by_period.condition: Living and playing on tailings-surfaced yards and roads, with fine asbestos and red dust settling on skin, hair and clothing.
A dwindling, isolated population living among demolished lots without services.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Mid-century working-class Australian dress for a hot climate: cotton dresses, shorts, short-sleeved shirts and sun hats; schoolchildren in simple shorts and frocks.
